output.title: Privacy promises are not the same as workflow control
output.body:
If you are considering AI in a small business, privacy promises are only one part of the question. A vendor can tell you where data is stored, how it is protected, or what terms apply, but that still does not answer the more practical issue: who can do what inside your own workflow once the data is there.

That is the decision I would focus on first. For any repeatable process such as invoice handling or customer replies, decide whether the AI is allowed to take action on its own, or whether it only recommends an action and waits for human approval. For money movement and other high-risk decisions, human approval stays mandatory. That is policy, not wishful thinking.

The reason is simple: privacy expectations do not control your approvals. If the workflow is loose, the safest vendor in the world will not fix that. If the workflow is tight, you can use AI without handing over the keys to the shop.

A simple question helps: will I see the input, the reasoning, and the recommended action before anything is committed?

Next step: map your most repeated workflow, mark the points where money, customer communication, or data deletion could happen, and decide which of those points must remain human-approved. If you are thinking about invoice handling, remember that Bareni’s accounts-payable demo is synthetic and the blocked payment was a manual simulation, not a real transfer. The point is the control design, not the theatre.
